title: A 31-year-old geometry conjecture falls — with AI agents exploring 100 trajectories
subtitle: Microsoft Research's Zhao Song and Xinzhi Zhang announced on October 21 a proof of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture, with a parallel paper from Bizeul, Klartag, and Lehec building on the same framework.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Microsoft Research announced on October 21 a proof of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture, a 31-year-old problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability. Xinzhi Zhang, a senior researcher in Microsoft's Machine Learning and Optimization group, worked with Zhao Song to bound the KLS constant by a universal number that does not depend on dimension — the central claim the 1995 conjecture made. The paper, 'An O(1) Bound for the KLS Constant,' first appeared on arXiv on October 1 with a revised version on October 4. A separate 32-page paper by Pierre Bizeul, Boaz Klartag, and Joseph Lehec, posted at arxiv.org/abs/2610.05474, builds on the Song–Zhang criterion and includes a paragraph describing its own AI use.

The methodology is what makes this story interesting beyond the mathematics. The team used a human-directed agentic workflow: AI agents explored roughly 100 research trajectories while Song and Zhang picked which ones to pursue and contributed the recursive method plus the error-accumulation bound. Microsoft Research reports that unguided AI runs on the same token budget did not get there. In other words, the AI was a search amplifier, not an author — it generated candidate paths at a rate the humans could not match, and the humans chose which path was worth the mathematical work.

This is the second major mathematical result in a year to credit an agentic AI workflow in the paper itself, and the practical shape of that credit is converging. Where machine-aided proofs of the past (the four-color theorem, Kepler's conjecture) outsourced a specific finite check to a computer, this generation of papers is outsourcing exploration — the step of asking what to try next. The KLS constant was ranked among the top open problems in applied and computational mathematics on at least one LLM-authored leaderboard, which gives the result a benchmarking value independent of its mathematical content: it is a data point for how far human-plus-agent beats human-alone on frontier problems.

A takeaway for learners: when a scientific paper credits AI, read how. 'The model generated candidate directions and we verified them' is a very different claim from 'the model proved the result.' The first says the AI was a research assistant with high throughput; the second would require formal verification artifacts most papers do not produce. If you are reading AI-assisted research in your own field, look for three things — what the human did, what the AI did, and whether the AI output was independently checked. The methodology section is where the real news lives.
